question: Why do we have seasons?
title: Why do we have seasons?
summary: Seasons come from Earth's 23.4° axial tilt, not from its distance to the Sun.

steps.title: The common misconception: distance
steps.narration: Earth is closest to the Sun (perihelion, about 147 million km) in early January and farthest (aphelion, about 152 million km) in early July. January is winter in the northern hemisphere, so distance cannot be the cause.

elements.text: Myth: “In summer we are closer to the Sun.”
In fact we are closest in early January: northern winter!

steps.title: The Sun and the orbit
steps.narration: The orbit looks like an ellipse here only because we view it at an angle; in reality it is very close to a circle. The distance changes by about 3% over the year, far too little to explain the seasons.

elements.text: orbit (seen at an angle: really almost a circle)
The orbit is nearly circular: the distance varies by only about 3% over the year.

steps.title: The tilted axis: 23.4°
steps.narration: Earth's spin axis makes an angle of 23.4 degrees with the line perpendicular to its orbital plane. All year the axis keeps pointing the same way in space (roughly toward Polaris); it does not swing around as Earth orbits the Sun.

elements.text: The real cause: Earth's axis is tilted by 23.4° and points the same way all year.

steps.title: June: north tilted toward the Sun
steps.narration: At the June solstice the northern hemisphere leans toward the Sun. The Sun passes high in the sky, the same light falls on a smaller area, and days are long. It is summer in the north and winter in the south.

elements.text: June: the north leans toward the Sun. Steep rays, long days: summer.

steps.title: December: north tilted away
steps.narration: Six months later Earth is on the other side of its orbit. The axis still points the same way, so now the northern hemisphere leans away from the Sun: sunlight arrives at a low angle, spreads over a larger area, and days are short.

elements.text: December: the north leans away. Slanted rays, short days: winter.

steps.title: Takeaway
steps.narration: Seasons are reversed in the southern hemisphere. That alone rules out the distance idea: both hemispheres are at the same distance from the Sun, yet they have opposite seasons at the same time. At the March and September equinoxes both get equal light.

elements.text: The south has opposite seasons. Tilt sets the season, not distance.
